items.new: But here is an artist. He wants to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting bit of romantic landscape in all the valley of the Saco. What is the chief element he uses? There stand his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as if a hermit and a crucifix were inside; and here sleeps his meadow, and there sleep his cattle; and up from that cottage over there rises a sleepy smoke. Deep into distant woodlands winds a mazy path, reaching to overlapping spurs of mountains bathed in their hillside blue. But though the picture lies entranced like this, and though this pine tree shakes down its sighs like leaves upon this shepherd's head, it would all be in vain unless the shepherd's eye were fixed on the magic stream before him. Go visit the Prairies in June, when for scores upon scores of miles you wade knee-deep among tiger lilies — what is the one charm missing? Water — there is not a drop of water there! If Niagara were only a cataract of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, on suddenly receiving two handfuls of silver, debate whether to buy himself a coat, which he sadly needed, or invest his money in a walking trip to Rockaway Beach? Why is almost every robust, healthy boy with a robust, healthy soul in him at some time or other crazy to go to sea? Why, on your first voyage as a passenger, did you yourself feel such a mystical vibration when first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the old Persians hold the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it a god of its own, the brother of Jove himself? Surely all this is not without meaning. And still deeper is the meaning of that story of Narcissus, who, because he could not grasp the tormenting, mild image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and was drowned. But that same image we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

items.new: It was an odd sort of place — a gable-ended old house, one side palsied, as it were, and leaning over sadly. It stood on a sharp, bleak corner, where that tempestuous wind Euroclydon kept up a worse howling than it ever did around poor Paul's storm-tossed ship. Euroclydon, nevertheless, is a mighty pleasant breeze to anyone indoors, with his feet on the hearth, quietly toasting them before bed. "In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon," says an old writer — of whose works I possess the only surviving copy — "it makes a marvelous difference whether you look out at it from a glass window where the frost is all on the outside, or whether you observe it from that sashless window, where the frost is on both sides, and of which that fellow Death is the only glazier." True enough, I thought, as this passage came to mind — old black-letter book, you reason well. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house. What a pity they didn't stop up the chinks and crannies, though, and stuff in a little lint here and there. But it's too late to make any improvements now. The universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted off a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth against the curbstone for his pillow, and shaking off his tatters with his shivering — he might plug up both ears with rags and put a corncob in his mouth, and still that would not keep out the tempestuous Euroclydon. Euroclydon! says old Dives, in his red silk robe (he had a redder one afterward) — pooh, pooh! What a fine frosty night; how Orion glitters; what northern lights! Let them talk of their Eastern summer climates of everlasting conservatories; give me the privilege of making my own summer with my own coals.

items.new: They say that men who have seen the world become quite at ease in manner, quite self-possessed in company as a result. Not always, though: Ledyard, the great New England traveler, and Mungo Park, the Scottish one — of all men, they had the least assurance in the parlor. But perhaps merely crossing Siberia in a sledge drawn by dogs, as Ledyard did, or taking a long solitary walk on an empty stomach in the negro heart of Africa, which was the sum of poor Mungo's achievements — this kind of travel, I say, may not be the very best way of acquiring a high social polish. Still, for the most part, that sort of polish is to be had anywhere.
